nameStory: The "Abbreviated" Button Slug Moth gets its name from having shorter, more compact wing markings compared to other button slug moths. The "button" part comes from the small, round spots that dot its wings like tiny buttons on a coat, while "slug" refers to its caterpillar stage that looks remarkably like a slimy garden slug.
description: This small moth is a member of the fascinating slug caterpillar moth family, easily recognized by its compact size and distinctive wing pattern. Adults have a wingspan of about 0.8 to 1 inch, with brownish wings decorated with small, button-like spots and abbreviated (shortened) bands across the forewings. The moth itself is fairly plain, but its caterpillar stage is the real showstopper – a bizarre, slug-like creature that seems more alien than insect. Like other members of its family, this species transforms from a peculiar, gelatinous-looking larva into a relatively ordinary-looking brown moth.

idTips.label: Wing pattern
idTips.description: Forewings are warm brown with distinctive shortened bands that don't extend fully across the wing, plus small round spots that feel slightly raised when touched gently

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small moth with wingspan under an inch – about the size of your thumbnail when wings are spread

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Overall brownish appearance with subtle variations from tan to chocolate brown, sometimes with a slightly fuzzy, velvety texture to the wings

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Weak, fluttering flight that seems almost bouncy – they don't fly in straight lines like many other small moths

idTips.label: Resting position
idTips.description: When at rest, wings are held tent-like over the body rather than spread flat, creating a triangular silhouette

habitat: Found in deciduous and mixed woodlands throughout New England, particularly where oak, cherry, and other hardwood trees grow. They prefer forest edges, clearings, and suburban areas with mature trees rather than deep, dense forest. The moths are often attracted to porch lights and windows in wooded neighborhoods during summer evenings.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, usually after mid-May when temperatures consistently stay above 60°F. Look for them at outdoor lights on warm evenings.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight time is mid to late summer (July-August) when adults are most active and easiest to spot. This is when you'll find them at lights or occasionally resting on tree bark during the day.
seasonality.fall: Activity winds down by early fall, though a few stragglers may still be seen in September. Caterpillars are feeding and preparing for winter at this time.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity – they overwinter as pupae in cocoons hidden in leaf litter and bark crevices. Look for the distinctive slug-like caterpillars on tree leaves in late summer instead.

funFact: The caterpillars of this moth are so bizarre they don't even look like insects – they're bright green, completely smooth, and shaped exactly like a lime-green gumdrop, moving by gliding along leaves like tiny slugs without any visible legs!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small brown moths at lights, but the abbreviated wing bands are diagnostic – other similar moths either have bands that go all the way across the wing or lack the button-like spots entirely. Memory trick: "Abbreviated" means "shortened," just like the wing bands.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "slug" moths, these insects are true moths (Lepidoptera) and completely unrelated to actual slugs – the name comes entirely from the caterpillar's appearance and movement. The scientific name "Tortricidia" means "little tortrix," though they're not closely related to tortrix moths either.
compareHints: As the only Tortricidia species in New England, compare it to other slug caterpillar moths like the Saddleback Caterpillar Moth, which is larger and has more contrasting yellow and dark markings. The Abbreviated Button Slug Moth is consistently smaller and more uniformly brown with its characteristic shortened wing bands that other family members lack.
